los.text: Explain the stages of a normal pregnancy compared with common abnormal pregnancies (include the main findings from a gynaecological and obstetric history and examination)
los.html:
Dating
  • From LMP (Naegele's: LMP + 1 year − 3 months + 7 days)
  • Confirmed by dating scan (crown–rump length, 10+0–13+6 weeks).
  • Term = 37–42 weeks.
Trimesters1st (to 13+6: organogenesis, nausea, miscarriage risk), 2nd (14–27+6: quickening ~18–20 weeks, anomaly scan 18+0–20+6), 3rd (28+: growth, fetal position).
UK antenatal care
  • Booking by 10 weeks (bloods: FBC, blood group/antibodies, HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, haemoglobinopathies; urine; BMI; BP)
  • Combined screening for trisomies (11–14 weeks)
  • Anomaly scan
  • OGTT if at risk (24–28 weeks)
  • Anti-D at 28 weeks if RhD negative
  • BP/urine every visit
  • Symphysis–fundal height from 24 weeks.
Obstetric history
  • Gravidity/parity (G_P_), previous births (mode, complications), current pregnancy symptoms (bleeding, pain, fetal movements, PV loss, headache/visual change), medical history, drugs, social.
  • Gynae history: LMP, cycle, contraception, smear history, PCB/IMB, STIs.
Examination
  • BP, urine, oedema
  • Abdomen: fundal height (cm ≈ weeks after 24 ± 2), lie, presentation, engagement (fifths palpable), fetal heart (Doppler/Pinard).
Abnormal pregnancyClues
MiscarriageBleeding ± pain <24 weeks; threatened (closed os) vs inevitable/incomplete
EctopicAmenorrhoea 6–8 weeks, unilateral pain, bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, collapse; empty uterus on TVUSS with +ve hCG
Molar pregnancyHyperemesis, large-for-dates uterus, very high hCG, "snowstorm" USS
Hyperemesis gravidarumSevere vomiting, weight loss >5%, ketosis
Multiple pregnancy, SGA/FGR, placenta praevia, malpresentationDetected on scan or fundal height

los.text: Describe the common complications of pregnancy (include anaemia, gestational diabetes mellitus and hypertension / preeclampsia)
los.html:
Anaemia
  • Physiological haemodilution
  • Threshold Hb <110 g/L (1st trimester), <105 (2nd/3rd), <100 postpartum.
  • Usually iron deficiency → oral iron (ferrous sulfate), check response at 2–4 weeks
  • IV iron if intolerant/late.
  • Risks: fatigue, PPH tolerance, preterm birth, low birthweight.
Gestational diabetes
  • Insulin resistance from placental hormones (hPL, progesterone, cortisol).
  • Risk factors: BMI >30, previous GDM/macrosomic baby (≥4.5 kg), FHx diabetes, South Asian/Black/Middle Eastern ethnicity.
  • 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks: fasting ≥5.6 or 2 h ≥7.8 mmol/L ("5-6-7-8").
  • Rx: diet/exercise → metformin → insulin (if fasting ≥7.0 at diagnosis, start insulin).
  • Risks: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, stillbirth
  • ↑ future T2DM (annual HbA1c).
Hypertension
  • Chronic (pre-existing or <20 weeks); gestational (new ≥140/90 after 20 weeks, no proteinuria); pre-eclampsia (new HTN after 20 weeks + proteinuria (uPCR ≥30 mg/mmol) or organ dysfunction: renal, liver, neuro, haematological, uteroplacental).
  • Pre-eclampsia: abnormal placentation (failed spiral artery remodelling) → endothelial dysfunction. Symptoms: headache, visual disturbance, RUQ/epigastric pain, oedema; signs: hyperreflexia/clonus. Complications: eclampsia (seizures → magnesium sulfate), HELLP, stroke, placental abruption, FGR.
  • Prevention: aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks if 1 high or 2 moderate risk factors. Rx: labetalol first line (nifedipine, methyldopa); definitive cure = delivery of the placenta.

los.text: Describe the processes and potential complications of normal and abnormal labour
los.html:
Labour onsetRegular painful contractions + progressive cervical change.
Stages
  • 1st: latent (to 4 cm; irregular contractions, effacement) → established (4 cm → fully dilated 10 cm; ~0.5 cm/hour or more).
  • 2nd: full dilatation → delivery of baby (passive descent then active pushing; ~up to 3 h nulliparous, 2 h multiparous including passive).
  • 3rd: delivery of placenta and membranes (active management with oxytocin: <30 min).
Mechanism (cardinal movements)Engagement → descent → flexion → internal rotation (to occipito-anterior) → extension (crowning) → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.
Factors ("3 Ps")Power (contractions), Passage (pelvis), Passenger (size, presentation, position: OP is slower).
Abnormal labour
  • Slow progress/dystocia (amniotomy, oxytocin; operative delivery)
  • Malpresentation (breech, transverse)
  • Fetal distress (abnormal CTG → fetal blood sampling, delivery)
  • Shoulder dystocia (McRoberts, suprapubic pressure)
  • Cord prolapse (emergency CS)
  • Uterine rupture (previous CS scar)
  • Preterm labour (<37 weeks: steroids, MgSO₄ neuroprotection <30 weeks, tocolysis)
  • Prolonged rupture of membranes (infection, GBS).
ComplicationsPostpartum haemorrhage (>500 mL; causes "4 Ts": Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin), perineal tears (3rd/4th degree involve anal sphincter), infection, VTE.

los.text: Describe the factors that influence teenage pregnancy, and the potential implications for individuals (parents and children) and public health
los.html:
UK context
  • Teenage conception rates have fallen sharply (>60% since 1998) but remain higher than much of western Europe
  • Higher in Wales than England average.
Influencing factors
  • Socioeconomic deprivation
  • Low educational attainment/disengagement from school
  • Being in care or a care leaver
  • Daughter of a teenage mother
  • Low aspirations
  • Poor sex and relationships education
  • Limited access to contraception
  • Alcohol/drugs
  • Sexual exploitation/abuse
  • Some cultural norms.
Implications for motherInterrupted education, unemployment, poverty, postnatal depression, social isolation, ↑ smoking in pregnancy, late booking, anaemia, pre-eclampsia, preterm delivery.
Implications for child
  • Low birthweight
  • Prematurity
  • ↑ infant mortality
  • Poorer health and educational outcomes
  • More likely to be in poverty and become a teenage parent (intergenerational cycle).
FathersOften young too; similar socioeconomic consequences.
Public healthCost to society; measure of inequality.
Strategies
  • Comprehensive RSE
  • Accessible confidential contraception (LARC)
  • Youth-friendly services
  • Raise aspirations
  • Targeted support (Family Nurse Partnership / Flying Start in Wales)
  • Easy access to abortion services.
Termination of pregnancy
  • Legal under Abortion Act 1967 (as amended 1990) up to 24 weeks on grounds certified by two doctors (most under ground C, risk to mental/physical health)
  • Beyond 24 weeks for serious fetal anomaly or grave risk to mother.
  • Medical (mifepristone + misoprostol; at home up to 10 weeks) or surgical.
  • Under-16s: Gillick competence
  • Encourage parental involvement
  • Safeguarding assessment.

los.text: Explain how the nervous and endocrine systems maintain homeostasis
sessions: BMS 1: Introduction to the endocrine system
los.html:
Nervous systemEndocrine system
SignalElectrical + neurotransmitterHormones in blood
SpeedMillisecondsSeconds to days
DurationBriefProlonged
TargetSpecific (synapse)Any cell with receptor
Homeostasis
  • Maintaining a stable internal environment via negative feedback: sensor → integrator (control centre, e.g. hypothalamus) → effector → corrects deviation.
  • Positive feedback is rare (oxytocin in labour, LH surge, clotting).
IntegrationThe hypothalamus links both systems (neuroendocrine): controls pituitary, ANS and behaviour (thirst, hunger, temperature).
ExamplesGlucose (insulin/glucagon), BP (baroreflex + RAAS), temperature (sweating/shivering + thyroid), osmolality (ADH + thirst), stress (sympathetic + cortisol).
Neuroendocrine cellsRelease hormones in response to nerve signals (adrenal medulla, posterior pituitary).

los.text: Describe the different classes of hormones and their mechanisms of action
los.html:
ClassExamplesReceptorMechanism
Peptides/proteinsInsulin, glucagon, GH, PTH, ADH, ACTH, oxytocinCell surface
  • Water-soluble
  • Stored in vesicles
  • Short half-life.
  • GPCR → second messengers (cAMP via Gs/Gi; IP₃/DAG/Ca²⁺ via Gq) or receptor tyrosine kinase (insulin, IGF-1) or JAK–STAT (GH, prolactin)
SteroidsCortisol, aldosterone, oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone, vitamin DIntracellular/nuclearFrom cholesterol; lipid-soluble, carried bound to proteins; act as transcription factors → slower, longer effects
Amines (from tyrosine)Adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamineSurface GPCRCatecholamines act like peptides
Thyroid hormones (T3/T4)NuclearLipid-soluble; act like steroids
TransportWater-soluble hormones free in plasma; lipid-soluble bound (TBG, SHBG, CBG) with only free fraction active.
Signal amplificationSecond messenger cascades amplify one hormone molecule's effect many times.

los.text: Describe the relationship between the hypothalamus and pituitary gland
los.html:
Hypothalamus (above pituitary, connected by the infundibulum/pituitary stalk).
Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)
  • Neural tissue.
  • Hypothalamic supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin → transported down axons (hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract) → released into blood.
Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)Glandular (from Rathke's pouch). Controlled by hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones carried in the hypophyseal portal system.
HypothalamusAnterior pituitaryTarget
TRHTSHThyroid → T4/T3
CRHACTHAdrenal cortex → cortisol
GnRH (pulsatile)LH, FSHGonads → sex steroids, gametes
GHRH (+) / somatostatin (−)GHLiver → IGF-1
Dopamine (−) / TRH (+)ProlactinBreast
Negative feedbackEnd hormones inhibit hypothalamus and pituitary (long loop).
ClinicalPituitary stalk compression → ↓ dopamine → ↑ prolactin; pituitary adenoma → bitemporal hemianopia (optic chiasm above).

los.text: Describe the anatomy of the female human reproductive system and the main functions of oestrogen and progesterone
los.html:
Anatomy
  • Ovaries (oocytes, hormones; suspended by suspensory and ovarian ligaments; ovarian artery from aorta)
  • Uterine (fallopian) tubes (infundibulum with fimbriae → ampulla, site of fertilisation → isthmus)
  • Uterus (fundus, body, cervix; endometrium, myometrium, perimetrium; usually anteverted/anteflexed; uterine artery crosses over the ureter, "water under the bridge")
  • Cervix (endocervix columnar; ectocervix squamous; transformation zone where CIN arises)
  • Vagina
  • Vulva.
  • Broad ligament, round ligament.
Oestrogen(granulosa cells via aromatisation of theca androgens)
  • Proliferation of endometrium
  • Development of secondary sexual characteristics (breasts, fat distribution)
  • Thin, stretchy fertile cervical mucus
  • LH surge (positive feedback mid-cycle)
  • Bone protection (closes epiphyses, ↓ resorption)
  • ↑ HDL
  • ↑ clotting factors
  • ↑ binding globulins.
Progesterone(corpus luteum, then placenta)
  • Secretory endometrium (prepares for implantation)
  • Thick cervical mucus
  • ↑ basal body temperature (~0.5 °C)
  • Smooth muscle relaxation (uterine quiescence in pregnancy; constipation, reflux)
  • Breast alveolar development
  • ↑ ventilation
  • Withdrawal triggers menstruation.

los.text: Describe the regulation of the ovarian and uterine (menstrual) cycles
los.html:
Follicular phase(day 1–14, variable length)↑ FSH recruits follicles → dominant follicle → ↑ oestradiol → endometrium proliferates. Oestrogen initially gives negative feedback.
Ovulation (~day 14)Sustained high oestradiol → positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation ~36 h after onset of surge.
Luteal phase(fixed ~14 days)
  • Ruptured follicle → corpus luteum → progesterone (+ oestrogen) → secretory endometrium
  • Negative feedback ↓ FSH/LH.
  • Without pregnancy, corpus luteum regresses (~day 24) → ↓ progesterone → endometrial spiral artery constriction → menstruation.
  • If pregnant, hCG rescues the corpus luteum.
Inhibin (granulosa cells) inhibits FSH.
Endometrial phasesMenstrual (days 1–5) → proliferative → secretory.
Normal cycle21–35 days; bleeding 2–7 days; loss <80 mL.
ClinicalDay-21 progesterone (7 days before expected period) confirms ovulation; COCP suppresses the LH surge.

los.text: Describe the maternal adaptations to pregnancy (Circulatory adaptations, respiratory, brain and GI changes; endocrine adaptations)
los.html:
Cardiovascular
  • ↑ plasma volume (~40–50%) > ↑ RBC mass (~20–30%) → physiological dilutional anaemia
  • ↑ cardiac output (~40%) via ↑ SV and HR (+10–15 bpm)
  • ↓ SVR (progesterone, NO) → BP falls in 2nd trimester, returns to baseline by term
  • Aortocaval compression supine in late pregnancy (left lateral tilt).
  • Flow murmurs, S3 common.
HaematologicalHypercoagulable (↑ fibrinogen, factors VII, VIII, X; ↓ protein S) → VTE risk ×4–6; ↑ WCC; ↓ platelets slightly.
Respiratory
  • ↑ tidal volume (~40%) via progesterone → ↑ minute ventilation → compensated respiratory alkalosis (PaCO₂ ~4 kPa)
  • ↓ FRC (diaphragm elevated)
  • ↑ O₂ consumption
  • Subjective breathlessness.
Renal↑ renal blood flow and GFR (~50%) → ↓ creatinine and urea; glycosuria; dilated ureters (progesterone) → ↑ pyelonephritis risk.
GIProgesterone relaxes smooth muscle → reflux, constipation; nausea (hCG); gallstones.
Endocrine
  • ↑ hCG (peak 10 weeks)
  • ↑ hPL (insulin resistance → GDM)
  • ↑ cortisol
  • ↑ prolactin
  • ↑ TBG (total T4 ↑, free normal)
  • Pituitary enlarges.
Brain/other↑ ventilatory drive, mood changes, carpal tunnel, skin pigmentation (linea nigra, melasma), ligament laxity (relaxin).

los.text: Describe the stages and stimuli that occur during parturition and explain the post-partum changes that occur after birth
los.html:
Initiation(not fully understood)
  • Fetal HPA axis
  • → ↑ CRH (placental clock)
  • → ↑ fetal cortisol
  • → ↑ placental oestrogen relative to progesterone ("functional progesterone withdrawal")
  • → ↑ oxytocin receptors, gap junctions (connexin-43), prostaglandins (cervical ripening, contractions).
Ferguson reflex(positive feedback)Fetal head stretches cervix → hypothalamus → oxytocin from posterior pituitary → stronger contractions → more stretch.
Cervical ripeningCollagen breakdown, ↑ water and hyaluronan (prostaglandins, relaxin).
Stages(1) dilatation, (2) expulsion of fetus, (3) placental separation and delivery (uterine contraction shears placenta; living ligatures of myometrium compress spiral arteries).
Post-partum changes (puerperium, 6 weeks)
  • Uterine involution (fundus at umbilicus after delivery, pelvic by ~2 weeks); lochia (rubra → serosa → alba).
  • Lactation: placental delivery → ↓ progesterone/oestrogen → prolactin (milk production) acts; suckling → oxytocin (milk ejection/let-down). Colostrum first (IgA).
  • CVS returns to baseline over weeks (diuresis days 2–5); VTE risk highest postpartum; ovulation suppressed while fully breastfeeding (lactational amenorrhoea).
  • Mood: "baby blues" (days 3–10, common, self-limiting) vs postnatal depression vs puerperal psychosis (emergency).
